item.title: A Lower Bound for Approximate Agreement with Send Omissions
item.dc:creator: Ittai Abraham, Gilad Stern
item.description: In approximate agreement, parties start with numerical inputs in $[0,1]$. Every nonfaulty party must terminate with an output in the input range, and their outputs must differ by less than a given $\epsilon>0$. Define the output span of an execution as the difference between the largest and smallest nonfaulty outputs. Approximate agreement requires this span to be less than $\epsilon$. item.title: Byzantine Approximate Agreement: Grade, Detect, Average
item.dc:creator: Ittai Abraham, Gilad Stern
item.description: The previous post gave a complete approximate agreement protocol: send the current value, remove the $f$ largest and $f$ smallest values, and take the midpoint. Each round halves the span of the honest values. Starting in $[0,1]$, reaching span less than $1/n$ takes $O(\log n)$ rounds. Ben-Or, Dolev, and Hoch improve this bound to $O(\log n / \log\log n)$. item.title: Approximate Agreement with Omissions: From Midpoints to Averages

item.description: The Byzantine approximate agreement posts start with a protocol that halves the span of honest values and repeat it to obtain a complete protocol. item.description: Synchronized clocks help servers coordinate. For example, servers with synchronized clocks following the same schedule can switch leaders at nearly the same time. A natural approach is for servers to exchange their current clock values and take the average. But messages take time to arrive. item.title: Designated Sets in Concurrent Simplex and Alpenglow
item.dc:creator: Ittai Abraham, Clément Burgelin, Antoine Murat, Joachim Neu
item.description: Recent consensus protocols like Alpenglow or Concurrent Simplex run two confirmation paths concurrently: a “slow” path with two voting rounds, each using a small quorum, and a “fast” path with a single voting round using a large quorum. The “slow” path can actually finish first because distances are not uniform in a geographically distributed system. item.description: How many parties do we need to decide after one proposal and one round of voting, when some faults are Byzantine and others are crashes? The answer depends on both the faults we must tolerate for eventual progress and the faults we want to tolerate on the fast path. item.title: Time Is Money: Incentivized Causal Transaction Ordering
item.dc:creator: Hongyin Chen, Xu Zheng, Jichen Li, Ittay Eyal
item.description: Front-running is a pervasive and costly problem on blockchains. Users earn rewards by publishing functional transactions that keeps markets efficient, such as arbitrage. But an attacker can observe such a transaction before it is ordered and publish her own ahead of it, seizing the reward and eroding users’ incentive to issue these transactions at all. item.title: Information-Theoretic Kuplex
item.dc:creator: Ittai Abraham, Sourav Das, Yuval Efron, Jovan Komatovic, Gilad Stern
item.description: Simplex is usually stated with signed quorums that anyone can forward and verify. Here we describe an information-theoretic version. Parties have authenticated point-to-point channels, but no signatures and no transferable quorums. Each party therefore acts only on quorums of messages it received directly. The motivation is practical as well as conceptual: avoiding signatures removes signature verification from the critical path. item.description: TL;DR Lutris is a hybrid distributed system protocol that integrates Byzantine Consistent Broadcast with a BFT consensus DAG to minimize latency of specific types of transactions. item.title: From Simplex to Complex
item.dc:creator: Ittai Abraham
item.description: Tendermint and Simplex are both leader-based BFT protocols for partial synchrony with optimal resilience and $3\delta$ good-case latency.
